text: Neutral-atom companies regularly announce the largest raw qubit counts in the industry, and that's genuinely true — but most atoms in an array and most usable, error-corrected logical qubits are two very different numbers. This lesson is about keeping them straight.

QuEra and Pasqal are the two companies most associated with bringing neutral-atom quantum computing to real users, and both build on the same underlying physics from the last lesson: atoms held in optical tweezer arrays, entangled via Rydberg blockade. Both offer cloud access, and both pursue analog modes — where the system evolves continuously under a programmed Hamiltonian for optimization or simulation tasks — alongside digital modes with discrete gate sequences, more like how other platforms are typically programmed.

Here's why large raw atom counts are genuinely achievable — this figure shows real, user-configurable atom layouts a neutral-atom processor supports. Because tweezers are generated optically rather than fabricated as individual physical structures, it's comparatively straightforward to project many tweezer sites and load atoms into a large fraction of them. That's a real structural reason this platform can report very large trapped-particle counts — it isn't a marketing trick.

But having a few hundred atoms sitting in a tweezer array isn't the same claim as having that many high-fidelity, well-connected, error-corrected logical qubits — and conflating the two is the single most important scalability trap in this part of the field. Gate fidelities for neutral-atom entangling operations have historically lagged the best superconducting and trapped-ion results. Atom loss is an ongoing issue, since atoms can be knocked out during trapping or during the excitation and de-excitation needed for Rydberg gates, requiring active reloading. And connectivity during 2D rearrangement — physically moving atoms to bring the right pairs together — takes real time and carries its own risk of losing or misplacing atoms.

Next lesson closes out this chapter: all four modalities you've now met — superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom — compared side by side, honestly, with the real tradeoffs each one is still carrying.
